utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber was not informed of any preliminary matters to be raised, therefore could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Radinkovic. Before we continue I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Ms. Edgerton will now continue her cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Radinkovic.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now yesterday we left off talking about the 1400 prisoners who arrived at Manjaca from Omarska, and I want to begin today on the same subject. What happened to those prisoners while they were locked in buses in front of the camp gate was that overnight some of the men, some of the prisoners, in the buses were beaten to death; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I and the personnel who were close to them didn't know whether they were killed by beatings or some deliberate execution. The policeman who was the closest to the site informed us that some of them were taken out and liquidated on the spot. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So what you're saying is overnight -- my question to you was about overnight while the prisoners were locked in the buses. So you're saying overnight, you're confirming, overnight some prisoners were killed; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was already in the morning, at sunrise, it was already daylight. What happened during the night no one was able to see, none of us was able to see. It was happening inside the buses. But by sunrise visibility was greater and we could see that one by one was taken out of the bus and ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you hear what was happening inside the buses? You must have been able to hear the screams, couldn't you? You were only 150 metres away.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not hear any screams, but the policemen on duty who were close to the gate of the camp were able to hear and they informed us that screams were heard, whether they were inside the bus or outside the bus, I don't know. But that was during the night. What we could see was that after sunrise some of them were taken out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, the witness said that before, he said: "We could see -- but by sunrise visibility was greater and we could see that one by one was taken out of the bus and ..." What did you say after "one by one was taken out of the bus and ..."?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're asking me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When there was more visibility, the policemen saw them being taken out and literally liquidated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you change "we could see" and "we saw" in the "policemen"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our military policemen who were the closest to the gate were able to see that. We were 150 metres further away in an enclosed space, we could not hear it or see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So maybe we'll move on a bit until morning time. So what you've been saying, what you've been talking about as well is when the 1400 prisoners were unloaded there were detainees unloaded who had been killed overnight, but there were also eight detainees that were brutally beaten to death. That's what you've been describing; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And your team, your security team, reported that incident to your command, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our security team reported that directly to me, and when I heard that such events were unfolding I went to see the camp commander urgently, asking to use the phone to report to our service, asking for reinforcement because our assessment was that it could escalate. So I personally was informed and I took steps to put an end to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you say you reported to your service, who did you specifically report to?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of security of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stevan Bogojevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So what you did was you went over and you used the telephone and you called your chief of security. Now, what I want to know is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is not what the witness said. He informed his commander and asked him to contact the person.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: He asked his commander to, yes -- pardon me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you informed -- when you say you went to see the camp commander, that means you went to see Popovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just said that I had gone to see the camp commander, Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic, Bozidar I think his name was. I went to see him only to ask to use his phone because we didn't have a telephone, he had one.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. So you called -- is it correct that you called Stevan Bogojevic and told him what was going on?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I told him what was going on and I immediately suggested steps to be taken, namely, that he should send a platoon of military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can I please clarify that. Did you call your commander by phone or did you go to see him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't go to see him, he was in Banja Luka. My superior was in Banja Luka, whereas the camp commander was in the next office. We should make a distinction between these two things. The camp commander was in the office next door, Popovic, and my commander was in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was mixed up during the last questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now -- so you've told us steps that you personally took in light of the crime that was unfolding in front of the camp. I want to know what the military and civilian police and the other camp staff did at that moment to try and stop what was going on in front of them?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately it was the military police who were doing it, the military police who were escorting the prisoners, they were doing these things. As for the military police, the military police served for the internal security of the camp, certainly not outside the main gate of the camp. They could not go outside and they could especially not get into conflict with the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm a bit confused --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I wish to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In your last sentence at the beginning you said -- this is what I read in the transcript, you said: "Unfortunately it was the military police who were doing it, the military police who were escorting the prisoners ..." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the civilian police was bringing these prisoners and escorting the buses, and the military police served for the internal security of the camp. They had absolutely no authority or powers or ability to go outside the gate and take any steps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- because they were in charge of securing the facility of the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Perhaps it was a slip of the tongue or interpretation issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you a very direct question. Why didn't you go to the fence and say: Hey, you guys, stop doing that. Isn't that a human duty, rather than to call someone who is at a distance of 20, 30 kilometres away -- I mean, I don't need authority if I see someone killing another person to at least say that he should stop doing that and not kill a second person, a third person, a fourth person. That's the issue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regrettably, three men who were commanders or something came to the gate and said, "Who do you think you are that you are standing in the way of a regular admission of these people?" Two of them came to the office and said, "We had orders from our boss and you have to do what our boss says." They mean their boss from the civilian police. So that ruled out any possibility for me to tell them: People, do your job the way you should, according to regular procedure, make the lists, et cetera. They refused it all. They said, "If you don't want to do what our boss says, we're not going to talk to you anymore." So I couldn't go to the gate and especially not remind them of their human duty and norms of behaviour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: First of all, these people who came to your office who referred to their boss, who did you understand them to be referring to? Who was the boss?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The boss was Simo Drljaca, the chief of the security centre -- security services of Prijedor, the chief for that region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton, can I just get a clarification here. Sir, you say you, the military police, were responsible for security inside the camp and could not do anything. When you phoned Stevan Bogojevic to send in a platoon of military police, what were they coming to do if the military police in the camp could do nothing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The military police didn't dare to do anything. They were not able to do anything. It was not in their purview. It was not within their authority. Their job was to provide security for that thousand or so people inside the facility and to prevent anyone from coming in. And I called in that platoon of military police, because I knew they were always available, in order to prevent this because these men had obviously run out of control. I don't know what their reasons were. I wanted them to put an end to it, and within a very short time, 45 minutes, they arrived. It was an intervention unit who had their own vehicle, et cetera, they arrived very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But I appreciate what you've told us, but that doesn't answer my question. My question is: If the military police inside the camp cannot or do not have the authority to intervene, by what right do the military police from somewhere else have the right to intervene where civilian police are involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the structure of command and control, the platoon of the military police within the 1st Krajina Corps is available. It's not a different police, it's just a different platoon which serves as a protection platoon for special purposes, special actions. They arrived ultimately to protect their own colleagues in case of an attack on the camp and also to put a stop to what was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The camp was not being attacked. It is the detainees in the buses who were being attacked. The military police in the camp said they had no authority to do anything. I don't understand how the military police from the platoon of the KK could have any authority. You're not answering that question unfortunately, and if you don't have an answer just say to me: I don't have an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an answer to that question because when that military police platoon came, that platoon of the reserve police, they placed their combat vehicle outside the gate. The platoon of the military police was deployed and the civilian police then accepted our conditions as to how to proceed, to make the lists, et cetera. That was the point of the arrival of that other police unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're talking about lists. I'm talking about stopping the killing of the people. Anyway, again I say you haven't answered my question and I leave it there. Madam Edgerton, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you said that the military police at Manjaca had no authority to intervene to stop that killing. What about the military responsibility to protect prisoners of war and civilians under the Geneva Conventions, didn't that oblige them to act at that moment to stop the crime unfolding in front of them?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's why that platoon of military police was inside, for the purposes of internal security, to protect those of us who were working there and the prisoners of war. I have to recall that a person becomes a prisoner of war once he passes through the gate of the camp, not before. They were in charge of protecting the prisoners inside the camp, certainly not outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you're saying that the Geneva Conventions in this case didn't apply because these detainees hadn't passed the gates of Manjaca before they were beaten to death?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can interpret it that way too because they had not been turned over to us yet and they were not logged in the book of prisoners. But as I said earlier, we tried to organise that as the rules of the camp governed involving the hand-over of the lists and the Geneva Conventions also regulate that kind of admission process.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, my question wasn't about my interpretation. I want to know about your interpretation. Are you saying that you and the military police at Manjaca had no obligation to act to stop the crime unfolding in front of them, according to some kind of regulations?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already stressed this. The military police inside, every policeman had his own place and a certain area of responsibility that he supervised and monitored. All that happened within the camp. He had no right under the orders to go outside. Everything related to security and protection related to the inside of the camp and that's what the Geneva Conventions governed. There were more than 2.000 people inside and they needed to be protected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, perhaps you should move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yesterday you told Mr. Stojanovic that prisoners arrived at Manjaca with visible injuries, and you said that at transcript page 31731 to 31732. And so on the subject of injuries to prisoners, it's also correct, isn't it, that prisoners were beaten by the military police coming to and from their interrogations; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, such things happened too. It was not standard practice and there were certainly no orders to do that, but individuals with bad intentions, with a desire for revenge, did such things.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And prisoners were also beaten as they arrived at the camp when they got off whatever means of transport had brought them, that the people who brought them would make a gauntlet for the prisoners entering the camp to pass through, and as they went through that gauntlet the prisoners were beaten; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, that did happen in the beginning, that is to say, until a selection was made of policemen who were providing security. Since we could not have insight into the files of these military policemen, what kind of persons they were, whether they had some frustrations, et cetera, they abused the situation and they did that. However, very quickly a selection took place or perhaps it would be better to say that a certain number of soldiers, policemen, were removed and people who could do this more professionally were brought in. And then these so-called gauntlets or whatever they were called - I don't know how the prisoners interpreted this - that was strictly prohibited then and no longer applied. I'm sorry, as for bringing people in for interrogations, that did happen. When persons were brought in for interrogation, then some policemen tried to mete out justice the way they saw it fit and they did what they did as they were bringing people in for questioning, but then we dealt with that too.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And prisoners were also beaten during their interrogations by the civilian police officers, the policemen you referred to yesterday who would come and work in the offices of the security organs; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, they applied that method, too, of forcibly acquiring evidence, if we can put it that way. We could hear these screams and moans. They applied these methods. Our team had no need to do that. We really worked in such a way that would relax them so that we could get certain information. Again, I say, unfortunately we could not affect their work. They had their own guide-lines or their own rules of conduct and they were not duty-bound to report to us, even if we were to give them certain recommendations.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And on top of hearing the screams and the moans of prisoners being beaten in the offices nearby you, you yourself saw the marks of being beaten on the prisoners you personally interrogated; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When a policeman or a patrol would bring in a particular person for an interview, an interview as we called it, then as professionals we noticed that there were fresh injuries on these people, that is to say, traces of blood and things like that. These people, these prisoners even interpreted it in the following way: He tripped over and fell and that's how he had a scratch or a bruise or whatever. That was done in order to prevent even harsher beatings later. Of course we found out very quickly who these policemen were who did that kind of thing and an express procedure was applied to remove them from the service; that is to say, they were no longer allowed to be there and do that job.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: They were military policemen; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military policemen from the security of the camp itself, literally. No one else had the right to enter this inner security compound.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put one additional question just to this topic?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You told us just now that sometimes people were brought in to the interview by you and you saw injuries. What did you do? Did you record them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We as professionals, I mean it is most logical, I mean from the documents that you have available here you can conclude that we did our work extremely professionally and the least we could do is record that or as a matter of fact we asked for medical assistance, rather we would send them to the duty doctor, or rather, the medical technician who would call in a doctor and who would treat a particular person's wounds and so on. What we did later, it is only logical, we asked for that automatically. From our sources who were among the population there, we found out who these soldiers were who did that kind of thing and that was against regulations and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting you. You went beyond my question. I want to know where these injuries were noted down on paper. Was it in the file where the interview was written down or was it somewhere else, and was it reported to your superiors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly the superiors were informed because they were the only ones who could allow for a replacement of certain policemen. It's not that my colleagues and I could simply chase them away --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You are not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- it went to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You're not focusing on my question. Did you write that down on paper and can that be found? And did you report in writing to your superiors? Not -- I'm not asking about the procedure of replacement of military policemen. How did you inform about the injuries and how they were inflicted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not on paper. I mean the paper was about the interview on a particular topic that we dealt with, so that didn't belong there. It's up the chain of command that we reported orally that this kind of thing was happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Not on paper. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you -- when you say you reported orally up the chain of command, you mean you reported to your superior Bogojevic at the corps command; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, because it wasn't a single case. There were several cases and then we concluded that certain policemen could no longer do that and we asked through the chain of command to have them replaced.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, just on the subject of the treatment of prisoners I want to talk for a little while about Omer Filipovic, actually, and I want to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it's under seal, Your Honours, we'll have to go into private session briefly to show the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So in fact --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact, there was no working water-supply for the prisoners in Manjaca camp at the end of July 1992 and no working water-supply when the 1400 prisoners from Omarska arrived and they didn't have enough water, did they?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just as they didn't have it, then we didn't have it either. We were there too, we didn't have any water and that's how water was brought to us also, in jerrycans. Unfortunately there was no system there. Later on this was taken care of and then it functioned and then people didn't go to fetch water any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, two minutes ago you told us there was good water-supply, no problem whatsoever. And now Ms. Edgerton puts to you that there was no water and you say: Well, we didn't have it either. That's not very consistent. It undermines the credibility and the reliability of your evidence. I don't know whether you are aware of that. To explain why there was not sufficient water one minute after you told us that there was sufficient water is at least something that would puzzle us. Any comments on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have a comment. That is to say, if there is no water for them, there is no water for us. So when water is brought for them, then water is brought for us too. That is the only interpretation. That is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To go on to another area, you talked in your written evidence about the suffocation of 24 prisoners from Sanski Most during their transportation to Manjaca and I want to ask you a little bit about that. First of all, you reported to your corps command the fact that these prisoners were suffocated during their transportation; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was our statement, that is to say of the military policemen who were in contact with the civilian police that brought in these trucks, or rather, these prisoners in trucks, that they literally suffocated because the trucks were covered with tarpaulin. So they were sealed, not to mince my words, and they simply suffocated. There was no oxygen and that is how the people who were weaker died.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Now, also in your written evidence you said that your orders -- actually, you said "our orders" were to load these prisoners who had suffocated back on the trucks. So I want to ask you a couple questions about that. First of all, since you were part of the reception committee that day you would know that it was Colonel Popovic who actually ordered the bodies be removed; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Popovic as camp commander gave that order but at our proposal, the proposal of the security organs, because they wanted at all costs to leave those dead people there, but we had our rules and there was no space for this to be done. And Colonel Popovic gave this order to load them on to the trucks and then to take them to Sanski Most and do whatever it was that they were supposed to do with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. So since this was your order I just want to get this straight. So no steps were taken to identify the dead persons, right? You just said -- you told Colonel Popovic: Load them up and take them away?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, that was a logical sequence because we took in only the living. We could not take in the dead. We did not have records as to who was left there, I mean during the hand-over -- I mean people's names were called out and one by one and of course we could not deal with the dead in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, witness, are you serious in telling us that because if you would call out persons that had died, that that's the reason just to do nothing, just leave matters as they are, let's get rid of the bodies? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it wasn't for us to deal with dead bodies because we did not contribute in any way that this would happen within the Manjaca camp. Quite simply, they could not have been taken in because they were not alive. I don't see what's in dispute there. Those were the regulations, those were the orders we received, and that is how we behaved. I think it was only logical for them to be returned to where they had come from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't this an extraordinary situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is an extraordinary situation, but we are not in charge of doing anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't it true that in extraordinary situations, the rules usually do not provide for a response which would then allow everyone to say: The rules didn't tell us what we had to do, therefore we left it to others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, we could not decide on our own. The moment we realised there were 24 dead, we automatically had to contact the chief of our service to report to him what was going on. We had no powers to make decisions independently one way or another. We were waiting for feedback from our superior command. They said along the chain of command we would inform the security services centre in Sanski Most to collect them and take them back to where these people had come from. We just carried out what was within our competence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, I'm looking at the clock, it's time for a break. Witness, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. We take a break. Could you give us an indication as to how much more time you'd need, Ms. Edgerton, after the break?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll check to be more accurate, but I think I'll use my estimated time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which was, let me -- two hours, 25.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll aim for two hours, 15, actually, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, if you take your time during the break, then we'll take the time to ask Mr. Registrar ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Until now you've used one hour, 27 minutes, that's net time. We take a break and we'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Radinkovic, we'll just continue where we left off, still on the same subject about the prisoners from Sanski Most. Now, can you tell us, you've already said that it was Popovic who gave the order to remove the bodies based on your proposal, so were you actually there when the bodies were loaded back on to the truck?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's -- the patrol of the military police who was on duty went outside, stood outside at the gate, and when the living were disembarking from the buses, the dead bodies were taken out too. I personally wasn't watching.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what about when the dead were loaded back on to the truck to be driven away, were you there or not?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't my job to leave the camp without any special need. If the military police was carrying out its tasks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, let me stop you there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- as envisaged --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The simple question was whether you were there when the dead were loaded back on to the truck. Were you there or were you not there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's an answer to the question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you wouldn't have seen that it was not only -- that loaded on to the truck were not only the people who had suffocated, there were men who were unconscious and there were prisoners who were very much alive loaded on to the truck and driven away. You didn't see that, did you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not informed that the living were turned back, because all the living were admitted into the camp, even those who had to be carried in from that transport.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, again, no one asked you whether you were informed. The question was whether you had seen it. Apparently you have not. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So if you -- if you --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now you told us that it was the civilian police who brought these detainees from Sanski Most to Manjaca camp, but you weren't there to see that either, were you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case, the civilian police was bringing prisoners from these municipalities, and I certainly wasn't there, I didn't go outside because there was no need.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you don't know, then, that it was actually members of the 6th Krajina Brigade who were among the people escorting these trucks where people suffocated to death? You don't know that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. We were told that the civilian police from Sanski Most was escorting them. That's the report we got, and the civilian police were present during the hand-over.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We'll go on to another area, and I want to go to a document that you saw during your testimony in the Karadzic proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's P2899.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you've had a look at this document -- I'll wait a couple of minutes. There we go. You've had a look at this document a couple of years ago. It's a daily report of your team dated 18 to 20 August 1992 to the 1st Krajina Corps on the interrogation of prisoners of war at Manjaca and the visit of a group of foreign journalists.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's go over to English page 4 and B/C/S page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So have a look at the paragraph at the -- it's your document, so have a look at the paragraph at the bottom of the page in your language and the bottom of the page in English as well. Now, it says you received a task from Major Stupar, which was the result of a telegram from the Main Staff of the Serbian Army. And in accordance with this telegram there was a joint -- a large joint meeting at Manjaca camp, representatives of the Bosanska Dubica, Kljuc, Banja Luka, Prijedor, and Mrkonjic Grad police services came to Manjaca, and there at that joint meeting Major Stupar and Vaso Skondric presented some tasks and instructions for joint work. So you remember the meeting, right, we talked about it two years ago?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I remember that meeting, we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. So having seen this document, let's move on to a related document, it's P223, which I also showed you two years ago. It's an excerpt from the diary of a Kljuc SJB police inspector who you knew by the name of Tore Gajic and these are his notes about that meeting. So just have a look at the first page. So he writes on the 20th of August you see that you at number 4, are among the people who sat with Stupar and Skondric and the camp commander to discuss, as it says in the document, the treatment and prominence of persons who participated in armed disturbances. Now, if you just go down under point 4, underneath your name, you see reference to: "Introductory remarks on the Serbian republic presidency's position were presented by Major Stupar." And then there's a note: "A list of 92 individuals, for whom there is no evidence of executing/participating in military activities, they are quite ill and their appearance is attracting attention from the media and humanitarian organisations." So this is what you understood the Presidency's position to be, right, you had to gather a list of individuals for whom there was no evidence that they had taken part in military activities, were sick, or -- and whose appearance is attracting attention from humanitarian organisations. That's what you understood; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how I understood it, but it was already the product of our work by that time. We had already identified 92 people of that kind and it was our initiative that these people should either be exchanged or allowed to go to third countries or leave the camp in some other way.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. So let's have -- just go over a couple of pages and have a quick look at your list.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's go over to page 5 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: At number 11 on page 5, you see a young man or a man by the name of Refik Salihovic and he was arrested on May 29th and he's sick with active tuberculosis. So this is an example of one of the people who you picked that fit the criteria you were given; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said it's not they who gave us the criteria. We had already produced these criteria ourselves. Following the work of the medical team day by day, it was established that a number of these people should be sent away to receive medical care, and that includes the number you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment. All right. Let's just go over and quickly look at another one. Let's go over to page 12 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On page 12 there's a fellow by the name of Denis Gromlic who was 17 at the time he was arrested, right, he was born in 1975. So that's another example of the type of people who fit these criteria; right? You're not arguing with that, are you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It fits that criteria perfectly and I have nothing to dispute. These are the facts.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So let's go look at one final one before we leave this document, let's go back to page 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you see the name Refik Dedovic at number 20? He's got kidney disease, born in 1934. Right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the name. I think you misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Refik Dedic, born in 1934.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me? Yes, I see that and he was supposed to be one of the first to go. That's only logical, because we had already transported him in an ambulance to the clinical centre. There was no dialysis available at that time. We just sent him away for medical assistance, and I believe after this he was sent to Geneva for treatment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Now, so when we talked about this document in the Karadzic case and I asked you what you understood -- whether this is what you understood to be the Presidency's position, to release those people for whom there is no evidence of executing military activities, that they're quite ill, and their appearance is attracting international attention, what you said was: Yes, you understood that to be the Presidency's position because Major Stupar came from corps command with that kind of position, the command position, and he must have received that on the basis of an order from the Presidency or higher organs. You can confirm that; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I confirmed then and I confirm now, Major Stupar and that crew who attended that meeting only confirmed the position that was passed along the chain of command from the Main Staff and the Presidency, specifically the president of the republic, that these people whom we had already suggested should go should be urgently released. It was their position and we had no consideration for public opinion or the international public, et cetera. The interest of the world public had nothing to do with it. We were interested in getting treatment for these people, including this boy who was underage.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, now, let's go to one last document, it's P4289.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it's dated 11 September 1992 and it's another document you saw two years ago. Now, this is a document from your corps command forwarding the contents of a telegram from the Presidency granting amnesty to 69 prisoners from Manjaca and Trnopolje, and three of them - just three of them - Gromlic, who's at number 6; Salihovic, who's at number 17 -- two of them are the names you discussed at the August meeting. So a small subset, a very small number of the names you discussed at that meeting are released; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course. We made a list - shall I call it a wish list? - of people who should go and the command was just supposed to decide which of them or if all of them would be allowed to leave in various ways, through exchange or release, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Radinkovic, this is only a token gesture -- whatever your motivation, whatever your personal motivation might have been, this is only a token gesture by your leadership to avoid international condemnation, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's their right and their policy that I didn't go into. We did our job professionally. And as for why the authorities decided what they decided, whether to score points with somebody else, it's up to them. It had nothing to do with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, what they decided, Mr. Radinkovic, was to hold thousands of non-Serb detainees at Manjaca until it was closed in December of 1992, releasing them only on the condition that they be sent to third countries and that was their policy, wasn't it? You were there at the time, you saw it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I participated in the selection. Military age, able-bodied men who were captured, regardless of whether they had a criminal record or not, were the most logical choice for being released to go to third countries, because it was not in our interest to release them and then have to fight them on the other side if they rejoined the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one question in relation to the last answer you gave. It may not have been in your interests, but what was the legal basis for sending them abroad if they would have preferred to go home, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Among them there are some people - I have to tell you this - who had expressed their intention, their willingness, to join the Army of Republika Srpska. That's a statement they made to the security organs. They wanted to join their neighbours and friends in the troops. We could not release them to go home because that was not safe, and the second safest option was for them to go to third countries where they would be given accommodation and means of survival. But we couldn't release them to go home. Physically it was impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you mean by "physically it was impossible"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was impossible. It would have been a sin to release them from the Manjaca camp to go to their own homes. If they had been on the receiving end of beatings even there, you can imagine what would have happened outside. So the most logical choice was to let them go somewhere where they would be given accommodation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which you switch in one minute from telling us that it was not in your interest, that they would become members of the opposite army; and then to say: Well, we protected them. What would have happened to them if they were subject to beating if they would have returned to their own community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, logically that was the safest place for them because it was impossible for outsiders to come in and harm them, which would have not been the case if they had been at large. God knows what would have happened if they ran into the military police or the civilian police, God knows how they would have fared. So the safest place for them to go was a third country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. A minute ago you said: "Among them there are some people - I have to tell you this - who had expressed their intention, their willingness to join the Army of Republika Srpska. That's a statement they made to the security organs." Now, first of all, I wondered whether they had expressed their willingness to join the Army of Republika Srpska because you then continue to say: "They wanted to join their neighbours and friends in the troops."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly. There was a certain number of people of different ethnicities in our army throughout the war, I mean Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I now better understand. You say they wanted to join our army but they would not be safe in our army if they would be there with their neighbours, and therefore it was better for them to go abroad. What about saying: Well, perhaps the army is not the safest place, perhaps you better go home and do not join our army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, but your conclusion is not correct. I knew there was a certain number of people who had even made written statements about their willingness and desire to join the army. This number of people would have followed a completely different procedure. That is separate from our position, from our opinion, that for some other people the safest place to go was a third country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not entirely clear to me now. Are you saying those who wished to join the VRS, were they sent abroad or is it the others? Because you said "some had expressed," whereas apparently others had not expressed such a wish. Now, which -- could you first deal with the ones who expressed a wish to join the VRS. Was there a completely different procedure for them or what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not a procedure. Quite simply, we documented their written statements and they even exist here at the Tribunal; that is to say, that was their decision, their wish, or perhaps it was their assessment that that was the only way in which they could get out, out of the camp, but that was for them. It was for us to send this on. In the meantime a certain order arrived stating that a larger number should leave including those, we included those. The army did not call them up in a particular unit. Of course we put them on this list and including 500-something people, they went to Sweden or wherever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you give them the option to go home instead of to Sweden?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We could not have given them that and it wasn't our mandate to give them that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In your statement we find some observations in relation to Dr. Enes Sabanovic, who you said was not an extremist, not at all. And I think you told that he was then in the reception committee. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is well understood. We received certain information from the civilian authorities in the accompanying documents that he was some kind of an extremist in Sanski Most and so on. However, through our operative work, intelligence, and working with the man himself, we came to the conclusion that he was an exceptionally honest and fair man, a good physician, and he provided assistance to his colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, when you found out that he was not an extremist and that he was an extremely honest man, what did you then do? Did he continue to work in the reception committee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he had -- he had semi-prison status literally. He was staying among the prisoners but he had the right to leave at his own request, even at his own request, let alone when somebody would come to get him out. Then our male nurse from the infirmary would come and get him and they would provide medication together and so on. He was a good man and we said that to our superiors too. No matter how much we needed him, that he should nevertheless be one of the first to leave, regardless of whether it would be an exchange or going to third countries or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but although there was no proper reason to remain in detention, he nevertheless, although with a special status, remained in Manjaca, as you said, semi-prison status, he was not released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, nobody was released except for the pardon that the president of the republic provided to certain persons. Only when we would receive information in writing to that effect from the president that he had pardoned someone or released them, then that person would be escorted by the military police and would be taken to a place where he would be taken over by the civilian structures; that is to say, no one could have -- I mean, it's for the sake of their own safety and security if they were to leave they could not move about safely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One final question. You referred to the Geneva Conventions several times. Are you aware that under international humanitarian law which we find in the Geneva Conventions, that there is individual responsibility which cannot be evaded by saying that you acted under orders? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everyone who worked on the team for dealing with prisoners of war had to study the Geneva Conventions, and I was aware of them, my colleagues were aware of them; however, war and conflict are one thing and all of this is -- well, I claim with full responsibility that we as human beings made a superhuman effort to make these people feel as safe as possible and we did our best so that they would be treated according to the Geneva Conventions if not 100 per cent, then up to a maximum. We were -- how should I put this? We were the ones who took care of the police and everything else regardless of all of these other things. We gave our contribution under the given circumstances and possibilities because there were also questions like supplies and we were not -- well, it was the way it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you telling us that because there was a war situation that it would be difficult to fully comply with the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, because you should all, all of you here should bear in mind that this is 1992 and that the population of Republika Srpska was hungry for the most part; that is to say, the supplies were very poor and so on and so forth. But we -- or rather -- no, not we, the camp command managed to provide as much as was possible at that point in time. That is why I'm saying that a maximum was given, the maximum of what was possible at that time. Let me add something else to this. Some people came and it was very hot, summertime, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm not going to -- I'm not going to ask you for further examples. If I understand you well you say: Well, in war time, Geneva Conventions cannot always be fully complied with. That's when you refer to 1992, when you're referring to the situation, when you said war is one thing, and I take it that you meant with that that in war circumstances you might not be able or that the Geneva Conventions should -- the application of Geneva Conventions should be adapted to the war situation. Is that how I have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I wanted to say that we made a maximum effort on our part so that things would be the best possible, the safest possible, and so on. As for other circumstances, we could not affect them. There was a war going on. That's what I was saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions in re-examination? Judge Moloto has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. Sir, we saw from the list of 92 people who were ill, only two were listed among those who were pardoned, the 57 who were pardoned. What became of the remaining 90 of the sick ones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They waited for the first exchange that would come or the first departure. The first group went to Geneva, I think, if I remember correctly. They were waiting for the following list, the following team, if you will, that was 520 prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Were they not being treated as priority because of their ill health? I see people are being pardoned and -- over them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We gave them priority, we who processed them and provided the information, we thought that they were a priority; however, the assessment of others who were above us was the one that was decisive who could go. It was for us to give a green light, but all departures were not based on our lists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How long did it take from the time that you received this position of the leadership before they were finally released, the 520?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Given the time distance, as far as I can remember it was about a month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And all of the 90 were amongst the 520?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, regrettably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And they were sent to third countries in that poor state of health?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they went there to be treated, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What means of transport did they use to go to third world -- countries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Buses, organised, a sufficient number of seats, too, so that they would not leave as they had arrived to us. They went through Croatia and then I don't know how they went after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, any questions in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Radinkovic, you remember you spoke quite a bit about this incident upon the arrival of a larger number of prisoners from Omarska, and you said that you specifically informed your superior according to the security and intelligence chain. Your immediate superior in the camp, Manjaca, in regular daily reports did he inform the superior command in writing about the incident that had occurred?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have any insight as to what the commander Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic said in his reports to the command. We were just duty-bound to provide regular reports at least once a week if everything was normal and, if necessary, even on a daily basis when such an incident would occur. So a dispatch was sent on the same day -- or perhaps a better word would be mail was sent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're explaining the whole of the system of reporting. The question, however, was whether in the daily reports Popovic reported this incident. Do you know whether he did or don't you know? If you don't know, tell us; if you do know, tell us what he reported.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was informed that he in his report accentuated that day and that development from his point of view, but to a different service, not the security service. I'm not aware of the content.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You as security organs, according to your own chain, did you objectively and truthfully provide information in these daily reports about the situation and about the information that you received while working in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. You may have noticed that each and every one of our documents is signed with a name and surname. We as security organs could have used pseudonyms too; however, we decided that we could openly provide our own names and stand before these people any day afterwards and say that we as security organs did whatever we could have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we move into private session for a moment now and the document that I would like to call up in e-court, could it please not be displayed, P233 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Before we do that. About the incident itself, did you report that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. There's a two-page report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Stojanovic, I'm looking at the clock, we are approximately at the time of a break. How much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another four documents, Your Honours. It would take 15 minutes, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take them after the break. Witness, we take a break. We would like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom. I see Mr. Lukic is not present. The Chamber wanted to pay further attention to the request to allow Sasa Lukic to examine witnesses. I do not know whether the presence of lead counsel Lukic is needed for that or whether you could provide us all the information because we want to have detailed information about qualifications, et cetera, of Mr. Sasa Lukic. I don't know whether you would like to call your lead counsel for that purpose because we might do it at the end of the testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it would be better perhaps, for this more detailed information, to take the details from my colleague Mr. Branko Lukic. I think that would be all right, although another colleague is working now in our Defence team room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, is it possible that Mr. Branko Lukic, your lead counsel, is -- will be present, well, let's say, in the next 20 to 30 minutes? Is he around?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll try. He's in our offices, Your Honours. We'll try. I believe it's realistic to get him here within that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. And if he comes, he should be prepared to give all details about Mr. Sasa Lukic. Then, Mr. Stojanovic, meanwhile please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We can now continue in open session, Mr. Radinkovic, and I should like us to look at one document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 07062, 07062. I don't think that's the right document. The number that I have, 07062 -- no, that's not the right document, Your Honours. Until I'm able to identify the right one, I'll move on to the next one. P0 -- P2881. That's the right document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radinkovic, could you kindly look at it. It's a telegram from the Main Staff of the Army of the Serbian Republic Bosnia-Herzegovina dated 12 August 1992. In this text we see that it's under the name of Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at item 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: "For the purpose of creating appropriate living conditions in the Manjaca camp, immediately execute the following ..." Now, look at item 2: "Provide adequate accommodation to the prisoners, meals in the amount of 2.800 calories per person per day, continuous water-supply for washing and for drinking, no less than 20 litres per prisoner, soap, and toiletries." Can you remember if you had occasion to read this telegram of the Main Staff sent to the command of the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can remember because in the accompanying document from the General Staff, or rather, the corps command and lower units it was always sent to us or there was an accompanying letter from the Presidency referenced so that we were able to see from where it's coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thus, did the administration of the POW camp at Manjaca have the ability logistically to meet the commitments that followed from this order of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, as far as I'm able to remember, it was not possible to meet all of these requirements because, as I said, many things were in short supply. There was a deficit of fuel and food and it couldn't be supplied from the corps command to the Manjaca camp. We did our best to meet these requirements, but some things were just not feasible. At that time it was not totally realistic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 4 of this telegram --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could scroll down so that after the Trial Chamber reads this sentence we could move to the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: -- it says: "All the prisoners who are wounded, sick, or handicapped are to be transferred to a special facility which is to be made into a prison hospital with the equipment for radiography and other diagnostic equipment for periodic x-rays for prisoners who have tuberculosis." Can you remember if work was done to implement this order of the Crisis Staff as well?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, work was done, especially because there was some inmates who had tuberculosis. Even before this order they were placed in a facility separate from other POWs, but it was technically impossible to place radiography equipment in that facility. In any case, they were not far from the clinic where they could be occasionally taken for x-rays and other procedures --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you are interpreted as striking off this order coming from the Crisis Staff, is that correct, or I see it comes from Mr. Mladic. If you look at page 51, line 8: "Can you remember if work was done to implement this order of the Crisis Staff ..." Did it come from the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It must be a mistake of the interpreter. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. The interpreter has answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 5 we read among the orders in this telegram of the Main Staff: "Immediately stop all sorts of mistreatment, physical assaults, and beatings of the prisoners." My question is: Was this a constant order of the Main Staff and your superior command?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a constant order. But this date coincides with some of our reports or initiatives that certain people be removed from their positions because they were unable to do their work properly, and it came as a confirmation from our chief commander to clear this situation up. And very quickly after this, the best possible order was restored.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you now look at paragraph 6, the Main Staff writes: "Review the possibility of releasing civilian prisoners, whereas the military prisoners are to be ensured the conditions that have been ordered." How did you understand it? How did you understand your job in creating the possibility for considering the release of some prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By that time we had already finished with a triage and we knew exactly which prisoners could be released, could be allowed to go free, and that's what I referred to when I spoke about some of them going to third countries, which was the safest option. And as for the others, we also made some proposals that they be exchanged or sent to third countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now could we please look at P2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we move to another document, I have some questions with respect to this, especially the last answer. Mr. Radinkovic, in the document under item 6 it says: "Take into consideration a possibility of releasing civilian prisoners ..." You told us that you didn't have any authorities to release somebody. And now explaining this item 6 you said -- you are talking about transferring people to a third country, but nothing about release. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can, I can explain with full responsibility. Regardless of the fact that this was signed by the commander of the Main Staff, according to our rules of service, the way things worked in the camp we could not release prisoners to leave the camp on their own. That's the way it was regulated, but we had already selected a number of people who could be allowed to leave the camp because we had concluded they were civilians and had never been involved in any military activity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Reading number 6 doesn't limit the release to release to a third country or prepare for an exchange. "Take into consideration a possibility of releasing ... the prisoners ..." Did you take that into consideration? Did you make any proposals to release civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we could not do that, it was not our mandate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have another question. Can we go back to the first page in English, please. I recall that you said: I can remember this document because in the accompanying document from the General Staff I saw it. You said: It was not possible to implement all of that, especially to meet all of these requirements because, as I said, many things were in short supply, and you mention fuel and food. How do you react? You had an order to provide the prisoners with sufficient food. What did you do when you realised that you're not able to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was more the job of the camp commander. Our job, the job of the security organs, was just to monitor to what extent it was being implemented. Our conclusion, therefore, was that it was not feasible to implement all this. It was certainly the wish of the camp commander to put this in practice, but the reality was different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And what did the commander do after having received this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean the camp commander?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the commander, if he received instead of 2.800 calories per person, if he received 1.500 or whatever, he must have addressed his superior command to urge them to supply the difference. I stress again, it was the month of September --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, don't -- don't go further.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and the whole Republika Srpska was suffering from deficits and shortages --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Don't go further. I just wanted to know what he did and you just said you suppose that he did something. You don't know if he reported back to the superior units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose he did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But you don't know --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- because as I told you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But you don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't go into his documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you report to anybody about this lack of sufficient food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, along our own chain of command we reported that supplies were insufficient, and if anything could be done as human beings, as officers, as troops, we should do something to improve this. But it's important that we did so on our part and I'm sure that the camp commander did as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was now asking about your action. You said: "Certainly, along our own chain of command ..." Do you remember that you reported in writing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In one of our reports, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just one follow-up question. Sir, if you look at page 53 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: He can't look at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, all right. But anyway I'm citing this for everybody else. Regarding paragraph 6 of this document you were asked whether -- and if I'm -- whether -- "Did you take that into consideration? Did you make any proposals to release civilians?" You say: "No, we could not do that, it was not our mandate." Now, not only is this document mandating you; it is actually ordering you to do so. So to say it was not your mandate is not correct, isn't it? Because this order gives you the mandate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The order was global --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, sir, let's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- if it was written that we should release --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's stop right there. This order did not only mandate you; it ordered you to do so, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In part, yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you were not right --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- but our command had to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you were not right to say you didn't have the mandate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, because we had also to receive from our superior command a confirmed list based on the list that we had prepared. We could not on our own do it based on the telegram sent down from the main -- the chief commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So are you saying that Mr. Mladic was not your command, was not your chief commander? He's the highest authority in the army, or he was, and he's given you an order to carry out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course we honoured and respected the fact that he was our chief commander, but I stressed that this document had come as an attachment to the order of the command of the 1st Krajina Corps. They had to state expressly: On the orders of the commander, release such and such people. That was not done. Not a single document was made ordering us expressly as security organs to release a specific number of people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So I should understand you to be saying that you did nothing about this order until you could get an order from your command, so this order didn't mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you can't say that it didn't mean anything because it followed from another order. We were given orders from the command of the 1st Krajina Corps and they were just citing this order as the source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just rephrase my question. You did nothing in reaction to this order until you could get an order from your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is my answer. That's the way we operated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Following up on the question of honourable Judge Moloto, could we look at P2909.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We were now looking at a document which says: Consider the possibility of releasing civilians among the prisoners, whereas the military prisoners should be provided with certain conditions as ordered. Now, look at this regular report dated 29 August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's see the next page in B/C/S and in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You say here, and it is stated on this report that you wrote it,

utterances.speaker: MR. RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: "Based on the telegram of the Main Staff, we have engaged all our forces in harmonising lists of prisoners of war which we" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we go to the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, let us look at page 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was trying to find out where you were reading, Mr. Stojanovic. I can't see where you were reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's on the next page in B/C/S and in English, the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The B/C/S page was all right and let's look at the English. It's the right page. And it will be necessary to eventually move to the next page in English in order to finish the paragraph. I'll quote: "Pursuant to the telegram of the Main Staff, we have used all our available forces to harmonise the list of prisoners of war which we have managed to finalise and to submit, along with the necessary details, to the command of the 1st Krajina Corps."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What are you actually saying needs to be done here?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a written confirmation of what I have been trying to explain. We have done all that we were able to, especially in view of the order given us by our commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In reviewing these lists, would it have speeded up your work to check first who was a civilian and who was a military person in order to be able to release some of them?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have already done that work, but after we received this order along with a copy of the telegram of the Main Staff, we reviewed our lists again in order to arrive at a finalised list of people who should leave the camp in accordance with the criteria handed down to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
