utterances.text: For instance, the people who were brought from Prijedor, Kljuc, and Sanski Most by the civilian police and placed in the POW camp, would it be necessary, before you arrived at some operative information through processing these people, to obtain also the opinion of civilian police stations if perhaps they had some other operative information about the persons who had been placed in the POW camp?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We insisted on that from the very moment the camp was opened, it would have been very helpful to us; however, some of these structures completely ignored us. And once they delivered these prisoners to the camp, they washed their hands of it completely and left it to us to make an evaluation and do the operative work in the camp itself for any information we needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, the document that I misquoted earlier --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could we wait for one second. Looking at this report and this list of 41 persons, Mr. Radinkovic, do I have to understand that this being pursuant to the order, that these are the civilian prisoners listed here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this time distance I cannot say on the basis of the names, but I assume that for the most part it is precisely those people that we assumed were not dangerous and were civilians and that they should leave as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because you were instructed to keep the military prisoners, isn't it, so therefore I'm wondering whether this list would contain any military prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've just said that I assume that it would be civilians primarily. Maybe there are some military men here too. It's not in the description. But anyway, if it is stated that way, I mean then it refers to that part of the order that we should primarily be sending civilians. So that would be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, another -- still in all the documents, including this order and your explanation as well, it turns out again and again that in a camp for prisoners of war you're detaining civilians. Here again who should be released or not, isn't it true that if you are a civilian, that you shouldn't be in a camp for prisoners of war, especially not if it has been established that you are a civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how much you followed my introductory remarks. Civilians were brought to us, even minors. We didn't ask for them, they were brought there. And upon entering the camp they became POWs. That is how they were registered and then the ICRC accepted that, and then of course there were civilians, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, you told us that you could not receive dead persons. You could receive minors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If they were on the list, we had to take them in; unfortunately, that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You referred so many times to the Geneva Conventions. First of all, do you know which of the Geneva Conventions deals with prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How could I know just now off-the-cuff?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then how are prisoners of war defined in the Geneva Conventions? Is it if they are offered to me, irrespective of health, age, et cetera, and if I put them on the list, they are prisoners of war? Is that the situation in the Geneva Conventions? Or is it -- are the regulations different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I repeat, we did not make the lists when people were brought into the camp. These were still people. Now, were they civilians, were they military? These are the rules of -- these are actually the lists that were made by the civilian structures. And then there were people who were minors, there were people who were of age, there were people who were ill, there were military conscripts, and there were even those who had committed crimes and all of that, they were brought to us. However, when entering the camp they were registered as POWs. That's the rule that we had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but is it -- of course I'm now questioning whether these are the rules of the Geneva Conventions on which you relied so heavily that you treated everyone in accordance with the Geneva Conventions, whereas apparently you have your own concept of what a prisoner of war is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asserted and I continue to assert that these -- I mean, well, the security of the camp. We - how do I put this? - we made a superhuman effort that it be 100 per cent application of the Geneva Conventions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- on our part -- I repeat, on our part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. The Geneva Conventions say that you may detain prisoners of war. But to detain civilians who had not taken part in any way in war efforts, civilians of all ages, would you agree with me that if they do not fall within the scope of prisoners of war of the Geneva Conventions, that you did not make a hundred per cent effort but that you rather defined yourself what you considered to be prisoners of war and then treated them as prisoners of war without having any knowledge or even it be established that they never took up arms, that they were just civilians, sometimes very young ones, sometimes very old ones? Would you agree that you have created your own Geneva Conventions rather than to follow the Geneva Conventions as they are adopted in 1949?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry that you interpret it that way. We, our team, had we conducted the selection process outside the camp in terms of who would be brought to the camp, it would have been quite different, but this was done by the civilian, the military, whoever, they compiled these lists and they brought in a certain number of persons to us. We were not the ones -- actually, later on we made our assessments and through our own work we proved what we proved, as can be seen from documents, that there were people who were underage, people who were ill, and everything else that you've already mentioned. So it's not that we imposed any rules of our own. We really made an effort to work within the boundaries of the Geneva Conventions, everything we could do in that situation under these circumstances. The people who were brought to us were brought to us the way they were brought to us. And the people who were brought in, they didn't wear uniforms. How could we know? There were no accompanying documents. It is through our own work that we came to the conclusion that things were the way they were and that people were who they were. Well, that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked you those questions because you said several times that you studied the Geneva Conventions. That was the basis for asking you these questions. Any further questions, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You - when I say "you," I mean the administration of the POW camp - before you carry out security intelligence checks, before you interview people, before you carry out a triage, can you know at any point in time who was a POW and who was brought there as a civilian and presented to you as somebody who should be checked and treated as a POW?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had such cases as well that certain units down the chain of command, before bringing in POWs they would mention the names and the places of arrest and so on and so forth, so that is to say that that kind of thing did happen but that was, say, 5 per cent -- well, to be very literal about all of this. On the basis of lists, that's how it worked for the most part. They would bring a list to that location and the names would be read out. In 95 per cent of all cases we had no information as to who it was that was coming in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, I mean what structure of prisoners was being brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Abiding by the definition of a POW, once you've carried out your checks did you say: In our view, this is a POW, and in our view this other person was brought here on wrong premises and is not a POW?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. And again I have to say that a great many people who were brought there, had there not been for these winds of war, they wouldn't have come to a POW camp in the first place. But after all, this was an umbrella to prevent their further suffering.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The interpreters could not hear the last sentence. Mr. Stojanovic, in my questioning it turned out that there was some -- a possible problem with what the definition of what a prisoner of war is. Now, you put the question to the witness: Abiding by the definition of a prisoner of war ... Could you exactly tell the witness and tell me what you consider the definition of a prisoner of war, from where do you take that, what is it? Because you're referring to the definition, which apparently there was some dispute about it. Could you tell us what you had in mind exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when I interpret the concept of a prisoner of war, I believe that a prisoner of war is a person who, as a member of an enemy army, at one point in time during operations is taken prisoner or has surrendered. And under this definition I include persons who joined the units of the enemy army at -- at a given point in time were taken prisoner or surrendered to the other warring party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that's how the witness understood it as well, then we could ask the witness whether his answer stands or whether he would like to make any changes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In which sense would I change this, the definition of a prisoner of war. Quite simply, abiding by the order issued when the camp was established, point 1 said that from the moment a person was brought in or handed over by a particular organ legitimately becomes a POW. That meant full stop for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I leave it to that. Any further questions, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was told, Your Honour, that the last sentence of the witness's previous answer was not recorded in the transcript so I'm going to repeat that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we ask the witness to repeat the last part of his answer, that's the part that is missing. Witness, I'm asking you now to tell us what you said and which was not recorded. You said: "But after all, this was an umbrella to prevent their further suffering." What did you say after that? I'm not asking you to say anything new but just to repeat what you then said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said -- well, this is a literal statement, umbrella, because that meant that they could certainly stay alive in that area as verified. No one could touch them or do anything bad to them. That was the sense of what I said when I said "umbrella," they were protected up until they left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you'd say whether brought in as a prisoner of war or not, it was good for them to be there because they were protected. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P3885, please, could we have that in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A document under seal, therefore not to be shown to the public. Can we deal with it in open session, Mr. Stojanovic, or should we turn into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that would be possible, but out of caution I would suggest that we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Ms. Edgerton, any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Radinkovic, this concludes your testimony in this court. I would like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you, put to you by the Defence, by the Prosecution, by the Bench. I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I just inform you that I have been informed that my colleague Mr. Lukic would be here after 1.30, that is to say, after the break. So I believe that he will be here and ready to answer all the questions you may have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest that we take the break now and that we resume at 1.30 so that we can first deal with this matter which is of some urgency. We will take a break and we will resume at 1.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, thank you for coming to the courtroom. The Chamber is considering your request to allow Mr. Sasa Lukic to examine witnesses, and in that context we have a few questions for you. First of all, Mr. Sasa Lukic, is he on the list, is he eligible for being assigned as counsel as far as you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't think that he is on 45 list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then if he's not, then of course we would have to look at -- because other team members who are on the Rule 55 list of course -- 45 list, I'm sorry, of course a lot of checks have been done in respect to them. And if Mr. Sasa Lukic is not on that list, I would like to know a few more things -- the Chamber would like to know a few more things. First of all, is he fully qualified to act as counsel in his home state?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he is, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And since when?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have CVs here. We tried to send it to you and to your staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So I tried to print it because it couldn't pass through --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's too heavy, that CV to -- no, no, no, I'm just kidding.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It couldn't pass -- yeah. If you don't mind, I would kindly ask the usher to just distribute and then it may be easier to talk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's easier to put further questions to you. I must say, I've got no idea, Mr. Lukic, about admission to the bar in -- I take it in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether -- what the requirements are, whether it's just a matter of exams or whether there is any traineeship which you would need to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, to be self-employed there is a special exam, but to work for another lawyer as he did previously --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- you have to pass bar exam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So he passed both, bar exam at 2012 and defence law exam at 2013.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I even see that he's a fast learner. I would wish that I would say that for myself, Mr. Lukic, but I see as far as I understand there's no language problem. I go from bottom up. Experience in criminal cases since --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- 2009. Is that before Serbian courts or is that before the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, he worked only as a case manager on Beara team --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- in 2007, but as a lawyer he practiced only in Serbia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- in front of the courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now you say experience in criminal law cases since 2009.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He took his bar exam in 2012. Could you tell us what the experience in criminal law cases were between 2009 and 2012?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. He had a lot, actually, because you can defend anybody if the sentence -- prescribed sentence is less than five years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah. So you don't even need to be formally admitted to the bar if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As a law trainee you can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Self-employed since June 2013. Yes, he worked in your law firm I see --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And although bearing the same last name, we are not blood related.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The last entry is an internship in 2007 at the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Where was that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For Beara, Beara Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then he has worked in your law firm, he is acting as counsel, whether fully qualified or for the smaller cases. Do you have any information about any possibly disciplinary measures --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- taken?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can vouch for him that he does not have any disciplinary cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any disciplinary cases against him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can tell you that at least at any moment in time he has at least 200 active cases plus new cases, so he's really --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's pretty scary, especially if you also have to deal with cases here then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just go through -- yes. Is the only reason why he's not on the Rule 45 list that the seven years do not -- the seven years of relevant experience do not apply?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now -- yes, and that would take some time because he -- even if you would take the traineeship time into consideration then it starts only in 2009 which would take him to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- 2016 before he has the seven years.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you thought about -- is he a member of the ADC? He can't be, I take it, if -- well --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He can be member of ADC although not on a 45 rule list --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because you have to be admitted to the practice --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- which he is, competent in criminal -- international criminal law without any years requirement -- no, it's also seven years required for membership of the -- full membership of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. He could be associate [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Associate, yes. Not a full member yet. Now perhaps you could remind me, associate members are also subject to the disciplinary system if anything would go wrong? Have you verified that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just -- I don't have it on the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I've never -- I've never heard that anybody who is not a full member who does not practice has any procedure against him since --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, I do understand that, but I don't know how the rules are. If you're an associate member and, for example, if you're not assigned as counsel but if you are acting more or less as counsel by -- through examining witnesses, whether you'd be subject to the -- certainly I take it to the rules of the ADC but whether you're also subject to the system of disciplinary procedure. We'd just like to know --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I should check, but probably yes. Whoever practices --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You know what we say to witnesses if they say "probably."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Probably, yeah, but I cannot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then I take it that you'll verify that and we might look into the rules as well. Yes, well, the last requirement for full membership is, apart from disciplinary proceedings, that the person involved is not found guilty in relevant criminal proceedings against him or her. That's -- I mean, I'm just going through the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, you cannot enroll into bar if there is active proceeding against you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But this is also about proceedings that have been resulted in a conviction. Would that also be a bar to be admitted to the bar?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It depends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It depends.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If it's -- if the time passes, then it can be annulled; but if it's something fresh, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only for the lighter crimes it can be annulled, not for grave crimes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If time passes --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But he's too young --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To be born in 1981, there's not much time yet to have passed since any possible convictions. Again, I'm not suggesting anything, but I'm just going through the list of what is required if you would become a member of the ADC and what the consequences are. Then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have no further questions, but we'd like to hear the position of the Prosecution on allowing Mr. Sasa Lukic to examine witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to see the resume, though I don't think we have any significant problems. The only issue that I can think of is as a member of the Beara Defence team, I think it's always safer if on issues of conflict of interest that the -- General Mladic should waive a conflict if there could be one. As we can imagine a conflict between Colonel Beara and General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But Mr. Lukic did not deal with anything substantial. He was a case manager on that case. He was not a legal assistant at that time, still being a student.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Don't you think that a case manager would have -- may have knowledge or may have -- which he could either use or not use in another case. I mean, even if you're not involved in substance, your privileged knowledge might cause a problem already.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, we can ask Mr. Mladic, but I don't think that there could be anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To be on the safe side that would be preferable.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, of course, waivers are certainly important, if I look at the rules of the code of conduct, but are not the final answer to -- so therefore it's not just a matter if I have a waiver then everything is okay. Then that should be borne well in mind. I remember the rules on that, I think it was in 33 or 35, I don't -- forgive me if I'm -- do not have them all --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only if to be fully informed, Your Honours and my learned friend, Mr. Sasa Lukic is on our team already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So if there was any conflict of interest --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You should have verified it already.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's for sure, so that -- you're pointing at something that should have been considered already in the past, but it's better to do it now rather than to forget to do it at all. So if you would carefully look at the rules covering conflict of interest -- I think it's not 33 or 35, it's somewhere in the 11 or something like that. It's the code of conduct which deals extensively with how to deal with a conflict of interest if it arises after you have already assisted one client. That's one. And the other matter still to be verified was what exactly? It slipped -- yes, the disciplinary -- the applicability of disciplinary --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, my colleague Ivetic checked. Disciplinary proceeding can be instigated only against a full member of the ADC --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and not to associate members.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not to associate members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently assuming that associate members are not acting, and of course what we are doing here is to make an exception and would -- we would then allow him to act. This information, Mr. McCloskey, does that change anything in your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Finally, of course, I think the Chamber has also some powers in this respect to -- as far as the right of audience is concerned, but of course that is not the same as disciplinary measures. I think we have received all the information we needed. We'll let you know what our decision is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we will do it quickly. Then is the Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We are, Your Honours. That would be Mr. Milenko Jevdjevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While we wait for him, Your Honours, I do have one procedural issue. I had identified some additional schematics with the witness during proofing and had advised the Prosecution and the Chambers of those, but two of those actually are not on our Rule 65 ter list. They are numbers 1D05361 and 1D05362, so I think I would formally need to ask leave to add those to the Rule 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections against adding them to the list, which of course is not a decision on admission yet?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon. No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then leave is granted to add 1D05361 and 1D05362 to the 65 ter exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, in your proofing note you are referring to a third document, what about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The third document is on the Prosecution's 65 ter list and therefore does not need to be added. That would be 31890.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I learn every day. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Jevdjevic. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, greetings to everybody in the courtroom. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Jevdjevic, one line was already sufficient to make me aware that you are very quick speaker. Could you please slow down when talking, otherwise the interpreters will be unable to interpret for us what you say. Mr. Jevdjevic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Ivetic. You find Mr. Ivetic to your left. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, sir. Could I ask you to please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Milenko Jevdjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, could you first tell us where and when you were born?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I was born on 11 December 1963 in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And where is it that you now reside, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I now live in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a few questions about your educational background, but I'd like you to please focus on just your military schooling and I'd ask you to give us a brief resume of the military educational institutions that you completed.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: In terms of military schooling, I completed the military high school in 1982, then the military academy for ground forces, specialisation signals in 1986, and the General Staff school of the Army of Yugoslavia in 1999 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I'd like to ask you about your education and training relative to radio relay communications in the army. Could you please tell us what specific training you underwent in this field?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: As part of the regular schooling at the military academy, as part of the regular subjects, we studied all radio relay devices and systems that the army had at its disposal at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did you have occasion to perform duties relating to communications through radio relay devices during your career?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At what levels did you perform such duties during your career?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: As an officer serving in the branch of communications I was first commander of the signals platoon, then commander of the signals company, then commander of the signals battalion, and chief of communications in the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I would like to ask you about electronic surveillance or radio intercept operators. What schooling or training was required in the JNA for those type of officers?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: In the course of my schooling and later when I served in the units of the Yugoslav People's Army and the Army of Republika Srpska, we underwent all the training necessary for us to successfully protect information passed on through communications equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting for one question. You said in the previous answer you were chief of the communications in the corps. Which corps are you referring to, Mr. Jevdjevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the 5th Corps of the Army of Republika Srpska established in 1997. That means 18 to 24 months after the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you've detailed for us the training that a radio relay communications or signals officer would have gone through and the education that you went through. I'd like to ask you about an electronic -- counter warfare -- counter-electronics warfare officer in the JNA, what type of training would that individual have to go through to attain that position?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Officers and NCOs and soldiers involved in counter-electronic warfare or radio relay reconnaissance were also supposed to go regular military schools and study these subjects and undergo training in units for counter-electronic warfare and radio reconnaissance.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in relation to the JNA system, how long did that training last for someone to be qualified to serve in a post as a counter-electronic warfare officer?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: In the former Yugoslav People's Army, there was a whole arm of the service for radio reconnaissance and counter-electronic operations. The officers who worked in such units went through the same training as I, just as the others who were in armoured units and other units. In the regular schooling there was a whole course dedicated to these subjects. In counter-electronic warfare units, soldiers who came to do their regular military service underwent a six-month training in order to be able to perform their duties properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to return to yourself again and your career. What ranks did you hold in the army during the course of your career?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: My first rank as an officer after completing the military academy was second lieutenant, and I finished my military career in the rank of colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When did your professional service in the military end?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, what occupation, if any, did you pursue after your military service ended?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: After completing my military service I found a job in Telekom Srpska company, where I continue working.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us what job or duties you have within the Telekom of Republika Srpska, what job or duties you had or now have?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I work on maintaining telecommunications systems and also supervise telecommunication services.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like to ask you to tell us where was your first military service post upon completion of the military academies that you've listed for us?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: After finishing the military academy I was appointed platoon commander of a communications platoon in the Uzice garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And what were the dates of deployment at that position?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I remained in that position for two years, and I was appointed company commander of a telecommunications company, also in Uzice.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. As a point of clarification, the transcript records you saying you were appointed a commander of a telecommunications company in Uzice. Are there telecommunications companies in the army or is that a --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Signals.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. The interpreters have corrected that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, did you eventually come to join the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what units in the VRS you were assigned to and during what time-period?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: In the Army of Republika Srpska I was appointed commander of the signals battalion in the Drina Corps. And after the end of the war or just before the war ended, I also carried out the duties of commander of the Birac Infantry Brigade in Sekovici, then chief of communications of the 5th Corps, then commander of the Visegrad Infantry Brigade in Visegrad, and I completed my military career as assistant commander of the 5th Corps of the Army of Republika Srpska for morale, information, legal, and religious affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you identify for us when it was that you joined the Army of Republika Srpska and in what position and then the date when you would have been appointed commander of the signals battalion in the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I joined the Army of Republika Srpska in the month of May 1992. I was appointed battalion commander of the signals battalion immediately after the establishment of the Drina Corps in November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just to complete the picture, then, from May to November 1992 where were you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Within a shorter period of time I carried out duties in Bosanska Krupa and the communications regiment of the Main Staff, the 67th Regiment of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay, sir, now I would like to focus on the time-period you were komandant of the communications battalion in the Drina Corps. Could you tell us what your duties were at that post?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: My duties were to carry out communications plan of the Drina Corps towards the superior command, that is to say, the Main Staff, and also to subordinate units, that is to say, brigades of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And how many other personnel were subordinated to you within the communications battalion of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: In the communications battalion during war time I had an average of 40 to 60 men. Out of them, about 20 were officers and among them there were about ten officers who had completed military schools for communication before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in relation to the remaining members of your battalion, what military training had they had in relation to signals or communications?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Before coming to the battalion, a number of soldiers received training in the regiment of the Main Staff and then were transferred to subordinate units. So a number of soldiers, young soldiers, trained signalsmen came to my signals battalion. A number of soldiers after mobilisation were trained by us at our battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have anyone working in the communications battalion of the Drina Corps as a radio relay operator that lacked either of the trainings that you have identified, who had not gone through one of the trainings that you have identified?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you describe for us what is the key difference between a radio device on the one hand and a radio relay device on the other hand?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: A key difference is that in essence one can say that with radio devices one establishes radio communication, whereas with radio relay equipment, radio relay communication is established. Basically, radio relay communication is directed radio communication. Most radio devices have antennae that radiate signals in all directions equally; whereas in the case of radio relay equipment, the force of the antenna is aimed only in a particular direction and that is how the signal becomes stronger and also protection of these electromagnetic waves and the communication involved is enhanced. One of the main differences is that radio relay communication, because of all of these things that I've already explained, can be considered to be far more protected and reliable than mere radio communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What radio relay devices did you have at your disposal at the Drina Corps for transmittal of signal with either subordinate units or superior units?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: We had three types of radio relay equipment: Radio relay equipment that was marked FM-200, then marked RU-800, and finally RRU-1.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And in relation to each of those radio relay devices you have listed, how would you compare or describe their age and technology level?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: FM-200 was the device that was about 15 or 20 years old at the time. The RRU-1 in that period of time was the most recent one, it was about ten years ago, whereas the RU-800 in that period of the war was already over 40 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall the operating frequency range of both the RRU-800 and the RRU-1 radio relay devices?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: RU-800 and FM-200 operated from 610 to 960 megahertz, and RRU-1 operates within a range from 235 to 280 megahertz.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what was the effective range of transmission of signal for these radio relay devices?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: In the rules and regulations, FM-200 and RU-800 have a range of up to 50 kilometres, whereas RRU-1 has a range of up to 30 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Are there any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- just to avoid any confusion, in line 11 of the current page you are recorded as having said RRU-800. I think you referred to RU-800, only one R, is that correct, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I should have referred to two R's, it's radio relay unit, so it's really RRU-800.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But the answer relates to RU-800.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness consistently used RU-800 and RRU-1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's the reason why I wanted to clarify --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's not what I heard but we can clarify with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, you're recorded as having referred to a radio relay device as an RU-800. Is that in fact how you referred to that radio relay device?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: RRU-800 is its proper name. Perhaps I've been speaking too fast. RRU-800. And for the transcript, RRU-1 works from 235 to 270 megahertz. That's what I said, not 280.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we get one more question in before the break, are there any atmospheric or terrestrial factors which can affect the transmittal of the electromagnetic signal from one RRU device to another RRU device?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you briefly describe some of them?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: There is a series of factors that affect the transmittal of electromagnetic waves and signals of radio relay equipment. It is meteorological conditions as well. So, for example, if it's raining or snowing, then that has a negative effect on the transmittal of electromagnetic waves. Also, the afforestation of the ground can have an effect on electromagnetic waves. Then also the quality of the land, the soil, if there is a high metal content, then that kind of soil sometimes prevents the propagation of such waves. Of course, the main barrier would be a physical barrier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I am looking at the clock, but I'm at the same time seeking one tiny little matter to be clarified. Witness, you said: "In the rules and regulations FM-200 and" then I take it RRU-800 "have a range of up to 50 kilometres, whereas RRU-1 has a range of up to 30 kilometres." Now, from my understanding, rules and regulations do not finally determine what the range is. Do I have to understand this, that the rules and regulations require that FM-200 and RRU-800 should perform at least well on the range of up to 50 kilometres, that is to 50 kilometres; and RRU should perform well at a distance of 30 kilometres? Is that how I have to understand it because --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is the boundary for the use of the signal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and what actually happened, how far the signal travels is -- can be different, perhaps even worse or even better than what the rules require them to do, how to perform at a certain distance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then, Mr. Ivetic, we'll adjourn for the day. And for you as well, Mr. Jevdjevic, we'll adjourn for the day and we would like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30 in this same courtroom. But I first want to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate -- well, that is your profession, isn't it, communication - not communicate in whatever way, through whatever signals or whatever waves, with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony given today or whether that is testimony still to be given tomorrow or perhaps even the day after tomorrow. If you understood this well, you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day and we will adjourn tomorrow, Wednesday, the 18th of February, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.
